name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Thermodynamic changes and specificity in gas adsorption

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the adsorption of gases on solid surfaces:

Statement I: During the adsorption of a gas on a solid surface, both the enthalpy (\(\Delta H\)) and the entropy (\(\Delta S\)) of the system decrease.

Statement II: Physical adsorption is highly specific in nature and always forms a unimolecular layer on the adsorbent surface.

Statement III: Easily liquefiable gases with higher critical temperatures are readily adsorbed by activated charcoal.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Thermodynamic Changes During Adsorption
Adsorption occurs because the surface particles of an adsorbent possess unbalanced or residual attractive forces. When gas molecules accumulate at the surface, there is a decrease in residual surface forces and surface energy, which is released as heat. Hence, adsorption is invariably an exothermic process (\(\Delta H < 0\)). Simultaneously, the freedom of movement of the adsorbed gas molecules becomes restricted, leading to a decrease in entropy (\(\Delta S < 0\)). Thus, the proposition that both enthalpy and entropy decrease during gas adsorption is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Specificity and Layer Formation in Physical Adsorption
Physical adsorption (physisorption) arises from weak van der Waals' forces, which are universal and non-directional. Consequently, a given adsorbent surface does not show preference for a particular gas, meaning physisorption lacks specificity. Moreover, under high pressure, physisorption results in multimolecular layers on the adsorbent surface. High specificity and unimolecular layer formation are characteristics of chemisorption, not physisorption. Thus, the claim that physical adsorption is highly specific and unimolecular is incorrect.

Step 3: Application — Effect of Nature of Gas and Critical Temperature
The extent of physisorption depends on the nature of the adsorbate gas. Easily liquefiable gases, which have higher critical temperatures, experience stronger van der Waals' forces near their critical temperatures and are therefore adsorbed to a greater extent. For example, \(1\text{ g}\) of activated charcoal adsorbs more \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) (critical temperature \(630\text{ K}\)) than \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) (critical temperature \(190\text{ K}\)), and even more than \(\mathrm{H_2}\) (critical temperature \(33\text{ K}\)). Thus, the proposition linking higher critical temperature to greater adsorption is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the decrease in both enthalpy and entropy during adsorption and the ready adsorption of easily liquefiable gases with higher critical temperatures are true, whereas the proposition attributing high specificity and unimolecular layer formation to physical adsorption is false.

answer.text: All three statements I, II, and III

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Homogeneous catalysis, catalyst selectivity, and zeolites

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding catalysis and solid catalysts:

Statement I: In the lead chamber process for the oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO_2(g)}\) to \(\mathrm{SO_3(g)}\) using \(\mathrm{NO(g)}\) as a catalyst, the reaction is an example of heterogeneous catalysis.

Statement II: Starting from \(\mathrm{CO(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\), using \(\mathrm{Ni}\) as a catalyst yields \(\mathrm{CH_4(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\), whereas using \(\mathrm{Cu}\) as a catalyst yields \(\mathrm{HCHO(g)}\), illustrating catalyst selectivity.

Statement III: Zeolites are microporous aluminosilicates with a three-dimensional \(\mathrm{Al\text{-}O\text{-}Si}\) framework that act as shape-selective catalysts depending on pore structure and molecular size.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Phase Criterion in Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous Catalysis
When the reactants, products, and catalyst are all in the same phase, the process is classified as homogeneous catalysis; when they are in different phases, it is heterogeneous catalysis. In the lead chamber process, \(2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NO(g)}} 2\mathrm{SO_3(g)}\), the reactants (\(\mathrm{SO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\)) and the catalyst (\(\mathrm{NO}\)) are all in the gaseous phase. Therefore, this reaction is an example of homogeneous catalysis, making the claim that it is heterogeneous catalysis incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation — Selectivity of Solid Catalysts
Selectivity is the ability of a catalyst to direct a reaction to yield a particular product selectively when multiple products are thermodynamically possible under the same reaction conditions. For the reaction of \(\mathrm{CO(g)}\) with \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\):
\(\mathrm{CO(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Ni}} \mathrm{CH_4(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)
\(\mathrm{CO(g)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}} \mathrm{HCHO(g)}\)
Thus, the claim that \(\mathrm{Ni}\) yields methane and water while \(\mathrm{Cu}\) yields formaldehyde from the same starting reactants accurately illustrates catalyst selectivity and is correct.

Step 3: Application — Shape-Selective Catalysis by Zeolites
Zeolites have honeycomb-like structures formed by a three-dimensional network of silicates in which some silicon atoms are replaced by aluminium atoms, creating an \(\mathrm{Al\text{-}O\text{-}Si}\) framework. Because of their microporous cavities and pores, the catalytic reactions inside zeolites depend upon the pore structure of the catalyst as well as the size and shape of the reactant and product molecules. Hence, the description of zeolites as shape-selective microporous aluminosilicate catalysts is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning catalyst selectivity with \(\mathrm{Ni}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) on \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and the shape-selective catalytic behaviour of microporous aluminosilicate zeolites are true, whereas the proposition classifying the \(\mathrm{NO(g)}\)-catalysed lead chamber oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO_2(g)}\) as heterogeneous catalysis is false.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Charge on sols, Hardy-Schulze rule, and micelles

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding colloidal systems:

Statement I: When a highly diluted solution of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) is added to a highly diluted \(\mathrm{KI}\) solution, the precipitated \(\mathrm{AgI}\) preferentially adsorbs \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ions to form a negatively charged sol, whereas adding \(\mathrm{KI}\) solution to \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution produces a positively charged sol.

Statement II: According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the flocculating power of \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) is greater than that of \([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}\) for the coagulation of a positively charged sol.

Statement III: Associated colloids such as soaps form micelles only above the Kraft temperature (\(T_k\)) and above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), and revert to individual ions upon dilution.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Preferential Adsorption of Common Ions
Colloidal particles acquire an electric charge by preferential adsorption of ions from the dispersion medium that are common to the colloidal lattice. When a highly diluted \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution is added to a highly diluted \(\mathrm{KI}\) solution, \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ions are in excess in the medium, so the precipitated \(\mathrm{AgI}\) adsorbs \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ions to form a negatively charged sol (\(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{I^-}\)). Conversely, when \(\mathrm{KI}\) solution is added to \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) ions are in excess, so \(\mathrm{AgI}\) adsorbs \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) ions to form a positively charged sol (\(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{Ag^+}\)). Thus, the claim regarding the charge reversal of \(\mathrm{AgI}\) sols is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Hardy-Schulze Rule and Flocculating Power
According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the greater the valence of the flocculating ion (the ion carrying charge opposite to that on the colloidal particles), the greater is its power to cause precipitation. For the coagulation of a positively charged sol, negative ions act as flocculating ions, and their flocculating power follows the order:
\[[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-} > \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}} > \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} > \mathrm{Cl^-}\]
Because \([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}\) carries a higher magnitude of negative charge (\(4\)) than \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) (\(3\)), \([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}\) has a greater flocculating power than \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\). Therefore, the claim that \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) has greater flocculating power than \([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}\) is incorrect.

Step 3: Application — Formation and Dilution Behaviour of Associated Colloids
Associated colloids (micelles), such as soaps and synthetic detergents, behave as normal strong electrolytes at low concentrations but aggregate into colloidal-sized micelles at higher concentrations. Micelle formation occurs only above a characteristic temperature called the Kraft temperature (\(T_k\)) and above a particular concentration called the critical micelle concentration (CMC). On dilution, the concentration drops below the CMC and these aggregates dissociate back into individual ions. Thus, the claim regarding the conditions for micelle formation and their behaviour on dilution is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the preferential adsorption of \(\mathrm{I^-}\) or \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) ions on \(\mathrm{AgI}\) sols and the conditions for micelle formation and reversion upon dilution are true, whereas the proposition reversing the Hardy-Schulze flocculating power order of \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) and \([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}\) is false.

answer.text: All three statements I, II, and III
